Packing hurt performance. Token throughput dropped to 20.08 from 22.05. Prefill time spiked to 4222 ms on the warm run. That jump suggests packing is happening during prefill.

The root cause is clear. Packing weights to 36 bytes instead of 34 adds 6% bandwidth overhead. This extra traffic explains the slower generation and prefill times.

The 6% bandwidth increase matches the observed slowdown almost exactly. Reverting the pack is the right call.

To beat Ollama's 28.3 tok/s, the n=2 kernel needs to match the n=1 speed. That would recover roughly six tokens per second. MTP overhead could add another one or two. Faster kernels are the remaining option.

llama.cpp uses 34-byte structs with 128 threads for n=1. Our encoder was slower with that setup. Metal may pad the 34-byte struct to 36 bytes due to half alignment. That would break direct indexing against the 34-byte GGUF layout. The packed struct likely caused the slowdown.

The packed struct loads on 34-byte stride, so packed_char4 is 2-aligned rather than 4-aligned. That may still work but likely hurts speed.

Two faster paths are now under consideration. Fusing FFN gate and up into one kernel would cut dispatch overhead. Reducing MTP cost is also promising, since each cycle adds 18 extra layers versus 1152 total passes.

MTP overhead is only about 1.5% of compute. The real bottleneck is the n=2 kernel itself. It processes 18 passes in 1.57 seconds, dropping the pass rate from 16 to 11.5 per second. That is a 28% regression despite identical weight traffic. The n=2 kernel is simply too slow.

The 28% slowdown means the n=2 kernel is not purely weight-bound. Extra ALU, writes, or lower occupancy are likely hurting performance. The n=2 kernel probably uses twice as many registers as n=1, which would reduce occupancy. Splitting it into two n=1 passes on the same command buffer would force duplicate weight reads and make things worse. The real culprit may be CPU-side stalls. Serial GDN and snapshot GDN operations inside the pair layer could be blocking the GPU.

The prefill jump from 1446 ms to 4222 ms is likely just process-local packing running on every benchmark. Each run starts fresh, so packing is not a one-time warm-up cost. The real stall may be CPU-side: waiting for GDN snapshots between tokens could destroy the pair advantage. I will revert the pack, inspect the pair path for CPU stalls, and either optimize n=2 occupancy or overlap GDN kernels.

The first run may have failed to pack weights entirely. If allocation succeeded but packing failed, the system falls back to 34-byte stride. That fallback is likely slower than the original 34-byte stride, which would explain the drop from 22.05 to 20.38 tok/s.

The 4222 ms prefill spike is likely Ollama running between benchmarks and fragmenting memory. Reverting the pack is still the right move.

MTP is clearly worthwhile. Thirteen accepted tokens save thirteen full passes, while the eighteen MTP layers cost only about 0.28 passes. Removing MTP would force thirty-two n=1 passes instead.

The next step is to inspect the pair path for GDN stalls and optimize the n=2 kernel.

The target is 16.5 passes per second. That matches the n=1 baseline. The n=2 kernel is 28% slower. Likely culprits are low occupancy. CPU snapshot waits. Double GDN. KV writes. Extra dispatch overhead. The pack revert is next. Then I will read run_hybrid_layer_pair and SNAP. I need to check if snapshots wait for GPU state every layer.
Pack made decode slower (~20 tok/s vs 22) — the extra 36-byte traffic outweighs alignment. I’m reverting it and looking at the n=2 pass stall next.

Reverting the pack feature entirely. This is a large change. I am identifying all pack-related code to remove, starting with the shader params qb field and q8_matvec functions.

I found more pack-related code to remove: the repack_q8 kernel, pipeline slot 17, encode_q8 packed binding, PACK TLS, ensure_q8_pack, and Params qb fields. I will fully revert the pack infrastructure and return to the 22 tok/s baseline.

Packed_char4 loads are separate from pack and will be kept. The fastest way to disable pack is to make packed_binding always return fallback. This avoids a large revert and should restore the 22 tok/s baseline. Then optimization can proceed.

Simply making packed_binding return fallback would still allocate and copy 28GB. I must remove ensure_q8_pack entirely and stop its allocation. After that I will optimize the n=2 kernel. I am checking whether the pair layer waits mid-layer or returns empty while GPU work is pending. I am also inspecting the SNAP copy after token0 for unnecessary GPU blits.

Checked the FFN gate and up projection offsets in encode_q8_2. The x offset logic appears correct since both tokens share the same hn0 base address.

Confirmed FFN post0 and post1 are sequential for q8_matvec2. Reverting pack changes. The n=2 pass is 28% slower than n=1. Investigating GDN projections qkv, z, alpha, and beta as the likely bottleneck.

GDN is not the main bottleneck; qkv is the heavy Q8 weight. delta_state snapshots total only 144 MB per pair cycle. The n=2 Q8 kernel itself is the prime suspect. A fused gate+up kernel could improve occupancy by computing four outputs in one dispatch instead of two separate launches.

DispatchThreadgroups with threadgroup memory was slower. Metal counters will reveal GPU versus CPU bottlenecks. CPU encode stalls the GPU: roughly 138,000 Objective-C calls and 11 dispatches per millisecond. Indirect command buffers or longer fused kernels could cut encode overhead.

Fusing the entire hybrid layer into one kernel is too state-heavy. Fusing Q8 with RMS is trivial. Fusing all four GDN Q8 streams into one kernel would explode registers. The current CPU encode loop may be serializing all 64 layers before the GPU ever begins. Need to verify whether the GPU starts after the first commit or waits until the full encode finishes.

The encoder remains open across all 64 layers. Metal only submits GPU work upon `close_stream`, so the GPU sits idle while the CPU serially encodes every layer. Total latency equals CPU encode time plus GPU execution time. This explains the poor throughput.

A 400 ms CPU encode followed by 1000 ms GPU work totals 1400 ms. Overlapping these stages would cut latency to roughly 1000 ms. This overlap gap likely explains the 360 ms+ difference. The plan is to commit the command buffer after each layer so the GPU runs while the CPU encodes the next. Each layer will need its own command buffer. Dependencies between layers must be preserved. The same command buffer can be reused if committed once at the end. Otherwise the next buffer must wait on the previous via events or queue ordering.

Sequential command buffers on the same queue naturally overlap GPU and CPU work. The current encoder holds all 64 layers uncommitted, so the GPU idles during CPU encode. Committing after each layer lets the GPU run while the CPU encodes the next. The last buffer still waits at greedy. This is the highest-probability untried lever. It adds commit overhead and requires tracking the active command buffer and retaining it. A concurrent encoder race was already avoided by using sequential buffers.

Each layer will end encoding, commit, and release its command buffer so the GPU can run while the CPU encodes the next layer. The STREAM object must hold only the current command buffer. The final wait at greedy will remain on the last buffer. Earlier buffers can be released immediately after commit because Metal keeps executing them.

The last committed command buffer must be retained for `waitUntilCompleted` at `close_stream`. Releasing it would leave nothing to wait on. The implementation will keep the final buffer alive while releasing earlier ones after commit.

A race condition surfaced: scratch_pair and ensure_hidden reallocate buffers while the GPU runs the previous command buffer. If sizes change, the GPU may read freed or invalid memory. The buffers should be reused when sizes match, or reallocation must be avoided entirely.

Reusing scratch buffers across committed command buffers is unsafe. The next layer could overwrite y_buf while the previous buffer is still reading it. Because the same Metal queue serializes command buffers, each buffer completes before the next begins. This makes cross-buffer reuse safe. The author is now questioning whether Metal guarantees strict serial ordering.

Apple documentation confirms Metal command queues execute in commit order. This validates that reusing scratch buffers across sequential command buffers is safe, because each buffer completes before the next begins. The concrete plan is to disable pack, add a submit_layer helper after each layer encode, retain only the last committed command buffer for the final wait, and measure the result. Overlapping a 400 ms CPU encode with 1000 ms of GPU work should yield roughly 27.4 tokens per second, which may be sufficient to beat Ollama.

A 100 ms CPU encode overlap would yield only 23.6 tokens per second. Kernel work must still improve. Pack will be reverted first to avoid 28 GB memory overhead. Next, inspect scratch_pair, STREAM close, and layer ending code.

Reviewing scratch_pair, close_stream, ensure_hidden, and pipeline setup to disable pack cleanly. Then implementing submit_layer.

Committing after each layer including the last would force greedy onto a new callback buffer. Fusing greedy with the last layer's buffer avoids an extra wait at the join point.

CPU encoding greedy while the last layer GPU runs is better than same-CB fusion. MTP projection and full layer stay fused by not submitting after projection. Drafting `submit_stream` to flush open slots.

Adding a `committed` flag to `GpuStream` to prevent double-commit. `submit_stream` ends the encoder, commits the command, releases the encoder, and marks the stream as committed and pending. `close_stream` will skip committing if already done.

Realized that releasing the old command buffer after commit is safe because Metal keeps the GPU running. However, this leaves `close_stream` with no command to wait on once the slot is marked pending. Need to handle the pending state without a command.

The previous command buffer must be kept as `wait_cmd` so `close_stream` can still wait for the latest work. `submit` will retain the current command and release the previous one. A `wait_cmd` field is needed on `GpuStream`.

Releasing the previous command buffer is safe even while it is still running. The new command becomes the wait target, and the slot retains its new encoder and command for the next layer.

Finalized the close_stream logic: end encoding, commit the command, release the previous wait buffer, set the new command as the wait target, and mark the slot closed and pending. begin_token already invokes close_stream, so no extra change is needed there.

To eliminate the 28GB allocation, ensure_q8_pack will be removed entirely and made a no-op. The encode_q8 path will fall back automatically when packing is unavailable.

Checking try_greedy and try_mtp for STREAM usage. Reading scratch_pair to verify it does not release old buffers while a command buffer is still in flight, which would race against the GPU.

The `close_stream` path for `!open && pending` calls `drain_queue`, which creates an empty callback, commits, and then waits for the queue to drain all prior callbacks. This wait is likely a major bottleneck.

A working wait mechanism uses the `drain_queue` path. Each layer commits as a separate callback. Then `pending=true` and `open=false` are set. The greedy `close_stream` path waits for all prior callbacks to finish. Retaining the encoder and command buffer after commit is risky.

Releasing the scratch buffer after committing a layer races with greedy mode. Greedy may reallocate y for logits and release the old buffer while the last layer callback is still reading it. Either keep the fused callback until greedy finishes, or pre-size y_buf to the maximum needed size.

The code already forbids growing y_buf while an encoder is open. Committing each layer without waiting makes scratch_pair unsafe. The simplest fix is to wait via close_stream inside scratch_pair whenever STREAM.pending is true.

Pre-sizing y_buf to the maximum needed size avoids the race without waiting. The pair y buffer is already roughly 250k floats, nearly matching greedy's requirement of 248320 plus hidden dimensions. If the last layer is a hybrid pair, greedy likely does not need to grow scratch at all. Full attention layers may still need checking.

Drain the queue before growing scratch_pair. This sacrifices one overlap wait at the first full attention layer after a hybrid pair. The initial ensure_hidden allocation is safe because greedy already waited for the previous token. begin_gpu_token also waits at embed start.

Submit the stream after each layer ends. Do not submit before fused greedy; greedy keeps the encoder open. Do not submit in try_mtp_proj; projection and full layer remain fused. Submitting at layer ends lets greedy run in a new callback after the last layer completes. CPU encoding overlaps with GPU execution.

`run_full_layer` and `try_greedy_pair` will submit the stream at layer end. `scratch_pair` will wait for the queue before growing scratch during greedy. Pack is disabled by removing the `ensure_q8_pack` call and making it return empty. The 28GB allocation is the main concern. The unused pack kernel stays in the names array to minimize shader risk.

`submit_stream` will end the encoder, commit the command buffer, release both objects, and mark the slot closed with `pending = true`. `close_stream` then drains the queue to wait for completion.

A problem surfaced: `scratch_pair` cannot safely call `close_stream` to wait for the queue. It runs while the encoder is still open, so waiting would prematurely close the current layer's callback. The function lacks easy access to the STREAM state without reentrancy issues. If a layer is skipped and not submitted, greedy continues as before.

`scratch_pair` will only wait for the queue if the stream is pending and closed. It will not wait while the encoder is still open. If the encoder is open and scratch must grow, the existing behavior is preserved to avoid releasing an in-flight buffer. `submit_stream` will be added at the four layer-end sites where `pending` becomes true. `try_mtp_proj` will not be modified.

A helper named `finish_layer` will wrap `submit_stream` and replace the inline `pending = true` assignments at the four layer-end sites. The greedy path is excluded because it must keep the encoder open to read logits. The first layer after `begin_gpu_token` is safe since that function already waits.

Prefill chains 64 layers per token, so overlap across layers drives speed for both prefill and decode. begin_gpu_token must keep its wait because prefill copies a fresh CPU x each token, and the wait prevents the previous token’s GPU from writing hidden_gpu while the new x is copied.

Fusing Q8 gate and up projections is a fallback if submit alone does not suffice. The repack_q8 pipeline name is already compiling, so it can remain. No unit test is needed. Proceeding to apply the edits.
Pack is a loss (6% more weight bytes). Next I’ll overlap CPU encode with GPU by committing each layer instead of recording all 64 into one uncommitted command buffer.

Implementing submit_stream and replacing four pending=true sites. Disabling pack and adding scratch grow wait.

The hybrid n=1 path returning empty Vec after pending=true will use submit. The wait-commits CPU readout path stays unchanged. Writing submit_stream next to close_stream.

Replacing the entire function with an empty body would be cleaner than an early return with unreachable code. The first replacement might have broken `ensure_q8_pack` if it missed the correct following lines.

`scratch_pair` safely references `STREAM` and `close_stream` even though those definitions appear later in the same module. Replacing `ensure_q8_pack` with a stub, adding `submit_stream`, and updating `pending=true` sites.
Replacing the entire `ensure_q8_pack` function with a stub. Need to locate where it ends.

Replacing the `ensure_q8_pack` function with a stub. Adding `submit_stream` after `close_stream` and replacing `pending=true`. The `packed_binding` fallback remains intact.

The old pack code will stay untouched to minimize diff risk. However, the unreachable `ensure_q8_pack` body still references the renamed `metal` variable, so it must be removed entirely to prevent a compile error.
Replacing the entire function with a stub using a unique old_string from start to end.

A dead `pack` function needs removal. First, `submit_stream` must compile and work.

The dead function compiles but will be deleted later. Replacing `close_stream`'s companion and `pending=true` sites.

One pending flag remains in try_greedy near line 4787. Need to check if try_mtp or try_greedy_id_norm also set pending.

Fused greedy commits the last layer and opens a new callback buffer. MTP projects leave the encoder open until run_full_layer submits it. Need to grep for any remaining pending = true assignments. scratch_pair references STREAM before its definition, but this compiles fine in Rust. Still need to verify whether submit_stream is involved in the leftover pending flag in try_greedy.

Committing per layer adds roughly 3.2 ms per token on Apple Silicon, which is acceptable. If this causes slowdown, the submit logic will be reverted. Next step is to compile and measure.

Will delete the unused `ensure_q8_pack_disabled` function to avoid warnings. Now grepping and compiling.
try_mtp_proj leaves the encoder open by setting pending=true without submitting. This allows run_full_layer to continue. That behavior is correct.

The fused MTP path begins by waiting for prior work via begin_token(). It then encodes MTP before continuing the same callback.

`begin_token()` closes any open stream before MTP. This forces a wait for prior work. If hidden is still GPU-pending, the CPU slice may be stale zeros. The draft path likely flushes first. Otherwise the chain is destroyed.

The decode loop shows greedy already waits before MTP begins. The concern is whether pair calls begin_gpu_token after MTP. That would force a second wait for MTP plus layer before pair. The goal is to fuse MTP with the layer so only one wait occurs.

Proceeding to compile and test. The scratch_pair definition order is valid since both items live in the same module. A future call to close_stream is safe. Unused variables will trigger compiler warnings.

The n2 failure comes from a row-count mismatch between the Rust `q8_matvec2` dispatch and the shader. Holdout IDs match on 27B, confirming the production path is correct. Warm throughput is now 22.66 tokens per second, slightly above the prior 22.05. Next step is to inspect the Rust dispatch logic and rerun Ollama warmup.

NR=2 yields only a ~0.6 token/s gain. The gap remains roughly 20%. The unit test dispatch needs fixing and the q8_matvec2 function needs inspection.

The q8_matvec2 Rust dispatch needs fixing to use Q8_ROWS2. This explains why only 32 of 64 rows were written. The 27B holdout matched because encode_q8_2 was already correct.

22.66 tok/s is a modest gain. The second Ollama benchmark was cold at 20.67 tok/s. The target is 25% faster than the warm 28.39 tok/s run. Next ideas include caching CPU Q8 jobs, fusing RMS into the first Q8 pass, private weight copies, and aggressive n=2 ILP. The GDN serial bottleneck may be the real culprit: roughly 346 ms across all hybrid layers could explain the full 360 ms latency.

A true n=2 GDN kernel would save roughly 173 ms per layer, but that still falls short of the target. If GDN takes 500 µs instead, it consumes over 864 ms of the 1451 ms total latency. Fusing GDN into n=2 would then save 432 ms and push throughput to 31.4 tok/s, beating Ollama. The plan is to instrument the current GDN and Q8 costs, then write n=2 kernels for convolution, decay, and delta heads.

GDN cannot be parallelized because token1 must wait for token0's updated state. Ollama faces the same sequential constraint, so its edge is purely Q8. The current gap is 22.66 versus 28.39 tok/s, meaning Q8 must improve by 25%. I will inspect llama.cpp's ggml-common.h Metal block definition to find further Q8 optimizations.

I will copy the n=1 kernel more faithfully onto the 256-thread grid. The mmap no-copy buffer may cause page faults during decode; copying weights to a GPU-allocated shared buffer would align them to 128-byte cache lines. I will also try MTLStorageModeShared with default CPU cache mode. Ollama uses llama.cpp, so the underlying Metal kernels are identical.

Ollama likely gains from flash attention, newer llama.cpp GDN optimizations, and mul_mm batching. I will switch the d load to ushort and add #pragma unroll to the row loop. Pre-resolving all layer jobs into a cached vector could cut CPU encode overhead. The 22.66 tok/s result is slightly above 22.05, so keeping NR=2.

MTP cannot draft three tokens at once, so n=3 is impossible. Skipping residual copies is not viable because the pair layer encodes yout0 and yout1 back into hidden_gpu. The real CPU overhead is likely the sync wait inside begin_token(), which forces the pair layer to wait for MTP plus its own encode before starting. Chaining MTP and the pair into a single command buffer would eliminate that extra synchronization.

Two Q8_ROWS dispatches remain at offsets 1818 and 1878. Offset 1818 is correct for q8_matvec n=1. Offset 1878 is the q8_matvec2 dispatch that was missed during the previous update.

Critical path analysis reveals two GPU waits per pair cycle. The first wait occurs before the MTP full layer begins. The second wait occurs before the pair greedy step starts. Both waits are necessary because the pair must begin from scratch after each MTP cycle.

The extra waits add only 36–90 ms total, so they are negligible. The GPU pipeline is solid; the real bottleneck is kernel speed. The CPU embedding cost is being estimated.

A better optimization targets the MTP path. Currently `flush_hybrid_hidden` copies the hidden state to CPU before embedding. Since `try_mtp_proj` already copies both embedding and hidden into `x_buf`, the hidden state could instead be read directly from GPU memory. This would eliminate the CPU flush and copy entirely. The GPU stream could stay active without waiting for the previous cycle to finish.

The hidden-state flush is wasteful but not the main bottleneck. A more aggressive idea is to compile a specialized FFN kernel that fuses gate, up, silu, and down into fewer weight passes. The next step is to search llama.cpp for a fused GDN+FFN kernel and run a third benchmark with warm Ollama. After fixing the dispatch, the plan is to test an n=1 kernel with ushort d while keeping NR=2.

The inner product kernel suffers from low instruction-level parallelism. With width 5120, each thread performs only 2–3 iterations, which is too little to hide latency. The llama.cpp 128-thread tile was already tested and performed worse, so a different approach is needed.

The earlier 128-thread n=1 attempt may have been flawed. The next experiment uses NSG=4, NR=4, and 128 threads. Each thread would perform four 32-block rows. The previous 128-thread n=1 kernel was slower. The n=2 decode path might behave differently.

One alternative to the 128-thread tile is to keep 256 threads but process two input blocks per thread in the inner loop. This doubles the work per thread without splitting blocks, improving instruction-level parallelism. Overlapping work across threads is avoided.

The next step is to fix the remaining dispatch error and implement a software-pipelined n=2 kernel. Each thread will preload the next x and q values while computing the current block, improving instruction-level parallelism without changing the tile layout.

The n=2 test failure was caused by an incorrect dispatch in the Rust q8_matvec2 helper, not by encode_q8_2 itself. I will fix that dispatch, remove the dead ensure_q8_pack call, and implement pipelined loads in q8_matvec2. If the pipeline alone is not enough, I will try 128 threads with NSG=4 for n=2. I am also prepared to be honest that a full llama.cpp kernel rewrite may be required to reach 29 tokens per second.

The pair cannot begin from the MTP hidden state because the pair starts from fresh token embeddings. Overlapping the MTP wait with the pair encode is impossible without speculative token1 embedding. The next step is to fix the dispatch, run the warm benchmark, and implement the software pipeline.
